dated_statements.statement: I started October 31st, 1983.
dated_statements.speaker: Roger Johnson

dated_statements.statement: (laughs) About 1968 in Idaho.
dated_statements.speaker: Bob Zybach

dated_statements.statement: So, at tidewater, we've accounts going back to the 1820s, people didn't seem to move in the daylight so much as they did with the tides.
dated_statements.speaker: Bob Zybach

dated_statements.statement: You might recall Bulletin 201 [McArdle and Meyer 1949]?
dated_statements.speaker: Jerry Phillips

dated_statements.speaker: Roger Johnson

dated_statements.statement: See that happened in 1936, and that's just when that started.
dated_statements.speaker: Jerry Phillips

dated_statements.statement: In the early 1930s you probably know that most all Western Oregon counties had huge acreages, that were tax delinquent.
dated_statements.speaker: Jerry Phillips

dated_statements.statement: So they decided in 1936 to offer that section of timberland within the Elliott Forest -- that was deliberate -- in lieu of paying their fire patrol taxes for those years.
dated_statements.speaker: Jerry Phillips

dated_statements.statement: So we're talking about 1927.
dated_statements.speaker: Jerry Phillips

dated_statements.statement: This is about 1936, for a dollar an acre.
dated_statements.speaker: Jerry Phillips

dated_statements.statement: So I figured if, when we started to work on the Elliott Forest, this is 1956, we worked from daylight until the sun went down.
dated_statements.speaker: Jerry Phillips

dated_statements.statement: So that way I can go back to the 1800s and see what things were like and where people lived and what they ate and what they did.
dated_statements.speaker: Bob Zybach

dated_statements.statement: is just think -- in 1950s, the State Land Board, for this ground we're driving through, their goal was to maximize annual revenue to the kids’ School Fund.

dated_statements.speaker: Jerry Phillips

entries.text: Tape 9-A. Interview with Jerry Phillips and Roger Johnson by Bob Zybach, with Amber Ross and Randy Wiest while touring the Elliott State Forest on December 6, 2017. Part 1. Adams Ridge, Tenmile Butte Salmonberry & Columbus Day Storm (47:42)

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Before we get started, Amber and . . .

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: This is it. Right here.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Oh, right here? Yep, sorry.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: . . . Randy and Jerry have already agreed on tape. We got that this will be recorded and transcribed. You'll have a chance to look at the transcription, if there's anything that needs to be corrected or removed or edited in some way.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Then it's apt to go anywhere. It won't be used commercially. It'll be used mostly on the internet for educational purposes. And hopefully research purposes too, so is that agreeable to you?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Sure.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: And for the record, what's your last name?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Johnson.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Roger Johnson, okay. So we're all in agreement. And you're being recorded right now.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Okay.
Tenmile. 2:22 Tenmile Lake, Work History & Boomer Colonies. No Photos.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Roger, real briefly, you've done reforestation work on the forest for almost 35 years?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I started October 31st, 1983.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: After other events.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Jerry, repeat the part here, we're going up to Adams Ridge?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: We are.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: That had been thinned out as part of the pre-1975 thinning program?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yeah, that's right.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: These trees are how old, about?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh, okay. So this is Coos Bay second-growth?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yes, well, essentially, but this side is also known as third-growth.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Third-growth, okay.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Stay on here, take a right here.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Well Adams Ridge itself, of course was never part of a state forest, because no Elliott land ever lay in Range 12.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: This will be in Range 12.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It was some of the land that we acquired from BLM through selection, back in about '61, around there. It was land that the federal government owed to us. It was selection. It was part of like, 6,000 acres of that.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: We chose -- I mean the State Land Board chose -- to have it here, instead of up a draw somewhere.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: A couple miles past that park.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: So in a sense, it has the same history, as the land that the State Land Board sold, to Elkside Lumber.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh. When the State Land Board sold it, that was the sale three years ago or something?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh, okay. So this went from BLM and changed to this -- in lieu of school lands -- added to the state, to Elliott's forest, and then thinned out once, and then sold.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That was the case. It was, well, some was thinned and some wasn't.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh- huh.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Because this is a fully stocked land. Of fir, good fir. The fact is, I guess it's true across all forests, you instinctively choose certain places that you like to look at, and it's so beautiful, that you don't want to clearcut.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Before your time.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So you're all right, in a few years, if they clearcut it?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Oh yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: (Laughs) I think we asked that on an earlier stand about that size: "Has it been thinned out?"

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: That's right.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: The decision now would be different than twenty and thirty years later. Roger, did you get any formal education in reforestation or forestry?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: An Associates from Southwestern Oregon Community College.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I went to OSU for a year but really couldn't afford to stay there.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Ahh (negative).

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Then I got a job with the state, restocking surveys, planting inspections, and that kind of stuff.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's the hard work.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Before we started doing these tours here, the last time I was on the Elliott was '69 or '70.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: (Laughs) It looks different, doesn't it?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah. My memory's kind of vague back then too. I was mostly doing Weyerhaeuser work and then I did BLM contracting in the 70s and so, further south.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah, I did plant trees on the Weyehaeuser Coos Bay Tree Farm.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Who did you plant trees for at that time?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I planted for Weyerhaeuser for the most part, for a small contractor out of California.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Straight ahead on this street.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Weyerhaeuser had union crews in those states.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Did they?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah, they did time studies on my crews in . . . 1974? They were just getting rid of them about that time, but I was working up in the Grays Harbor area.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah. The crew I was working on had openings because the guys they had working for them got caught by immigration.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Ah-ha.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: They weren't allowed in the States.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I remember the first Mexican tree planters.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Oh yeah?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah. (laughs) About 1968 in Idaho.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah we used the Shutter Creek [Correctional Institution] crews to do some planting and a lot of trapping over the last twenty years.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh. There's a deer. Now when you're talking about trapping, you're talking about boomer?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah, mountain beaver. Yeah, in the ‘70s they pretty much devastated a lot of the early plantations in the Forest. When I arrived there they were processing 10,000 acres. Stands that hadn't been successful through there. Something to do with mountain beaver and salmonberry.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: 10,000 acres?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yep.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: On the Elliott?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yep.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow. We did lots of boomer trapping up in Lincoln County but the populations of boomers that I've seen, the heaviest anywhere, are the Elliott . . .

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: . . . and Lincoln County.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I think [Township] 23 [Range 10] in the Elliott has the highest population in the world.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Wow [sees parked vehicle]. That’s been parked there for a couple of weeks. We don't know where they’re headed though.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: They had really extensive notes on the boomer damage, and even one damaging a surveyor worker!

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I think they were first noted by Lewis and Clark.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: (Laughs)

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well, the Indians were wearing them as robes, so that's what we were having the discussion before -- whether the boomer -- whether they were persistent; and when we went in to plant, because of the conversions [industrial alder to fir projects], we were finding on the Yaquina River and stuff, that basically they set out these colonies, and these colonies didn't have fir in the first place.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Boomers survive just fine on sword fern.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yep.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Because they were planning for those hurricanes.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: To them it was like pepperoni pizza! (laughter)

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: That's what it seems like they must, when the trees are young, they get rid of them, and then they persist.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: They'll climb trees.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: For a while.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah. For a foot or two.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I'd say . . .

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Ten.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Ten feet?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: For a whistle tree.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Boomers could climb ten foot in a tree?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yep, strip all the limbs off and top it.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow. So their basic strategy is to keep from being shaded out so they got food.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: You can live under that condition, a fairly wide space probably. But . . .

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Mm-hmm (affirmative). If they're totally closed in, they have nothing to do except chew the bark off the roots of trees.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So they can persist in a fairly closed canopy?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Not for very long.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah, I've never seen them there.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: They starve to death after a while.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So these patches in which you went in to plant, and they had to be replanted, weren't solid stands of fir before, they were boomer colonies?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: They may have been a Douglas fir with alder. Hardwoods lose their leaves, then they seem to be better habitat.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Right along the West Fork they have a colony.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: They're really not far from the Elkhorn Ranch, but they've been there forever. It's completely alders.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Aha. So there are openings in the forest, and wildlife habitat openings, that have been persistent because of the boomer colony.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Well, there's an interaction there.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: That was one thing I talked to my contacts was about boomer colonies, and then Jerry was saying part of the reason is all the bobcat trapping and coyotes and stuff that would be their enemies, but possibly the Indians . . .

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yep.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: . . . must have eaten them -- but they also, we know they skinned them for their hides and prized them.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: It seems like these might be hunting grounds that maybe -- thinned the populations and kept them down?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I don't know for sure on that.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Go right?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah, stay right.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: And then it will be the stand in the field there.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Stay on the main road from there up. It's at the top of the hill basically.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: You asked a question I just realized. I don't know, do you know how the Indians actually, did they shoot them with arrows? How did they catch them?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Probably by hands and rocks and arrows. They had traps.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: They're really hard to see.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: They come out mostly at night.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: They must have trapped them somehow.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah, that would be . . . I would guess over a several thousand year period that they had every way possible of getting them.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah, I suppose.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Every once in a while, you'll see them out scurrying around.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Like, they're going through their colony and that disturbs them or something.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Not usually.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: No, but occasionally.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I've seen one or two in the day -- and that's Tenmile Lake off to the right.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Tenmile Lake?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah, it flooded. That Shutter’s arm of Tenmile Lake flooded real bad. It backs up into the draw there in the winter when it rains a lot. I've seen one or two [boomer] in the daytime, but that's why I was asking how they got them because I don't think that you're going to see them in the day time enough to get any.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: This right here, one thing we've found working with the Coquilles, with Don Ivy . . .

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Mm-hmm (affirmative).

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: . . . we've found out that they're basically, the boundary line between the different tribes, and even the language groups, was the head of tidewater.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Really?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So, at tidewater, we've accounts going back to the 1820s, people didn't seem to move in the daylight so much as they did with the tides.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Because they're moving in and out with the canoes on the tides.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So operating in the middle of the night was nothing unusual for them. Then on the other side, above tidewater, it was all daylight and dark like we do today. But in the tidelands it was all driven by the moon.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Wow. I suppose if they actually kept going out in the moonlight at night? I guess that might be right. If you're patient enough to sit there long enough, they won't smell you.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: They had elk dogs too.

entries.text: It's not that it's staying dormant. It has little pieces sticking up like that, that aren't obvious when you look at it. They're ready to take off. They persist where light gets through the canopy.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: One reason we're looking at this and discussing it is this is one of the thickest patches on the ridgeline on the forest.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Mm-hmm (affirmative).

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: And that's the question: If it's persistent, that means that people were probably using the salmonberry 200 years ago -- but if it's just spreading?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: That would mean that since you started logging in it, you would . . .

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: No, it was here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh, okay.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: That’s one we couldn't kill it or freeze it out.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Ah-hah. Salmonberry and boomers sometimes co-exist close to water, but on ridgelines I wouldn't think that would be . . .?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I don't think there's any place we haven't found a boomer in something.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Even high?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Ridgetops.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's right.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Just about everywhere.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: They've got to be within 50 or 100 feet of water don't they?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: You know, they seem to get water somewhere anyway.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I don't know if they're seasonal or if they move from top down with the weather or not.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh. That would make sense. So in the winter they could be up on the ridgeline.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Mm-hmm (affirmative).

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: And then in the summer move down.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Right. I don’t think they would move very far -- but in some part of their run they go through, of course, a water source.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: So, where's the patch going to be?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: On the right hand side.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: From where again?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: This is where the salmonberry was?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I'd go a little further in there.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Now this is Tenmile Ridge?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Tenmile Butte.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Tenmile Butte, okay.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: This had all the homesteaders.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Is that a homestead?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: This whole area.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Might as well stop here and turn around here. Turn around, yeah. Not the other way though.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Himalayan blackberry was brought in by the pioneers too, and it's a bit of a problem.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's right.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It was sold: “Guaranteed to grow!”

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Bob, let me know what areas of interest you want me to collect photos of.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay. I think this is definitely one. Tenmile Butte salmonberry patch. We've had a lot of discussion on it.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: You want to get out here?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Not necessarily. We've been getting out in spots and taking photos but the recorder . . .

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: . . . stays here?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well, this is a Black Friday special deal. The other one I had was from the ‘90s, it was operating real good until it stopped.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Not going to record the sound outside?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I cut that out. It won't record for a very long distance. And then it's tough to get in and out in this [vehicle], isn’t it Jerry? (Laughs)

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Mm-hmm (affirmative). It is. (Laughs)

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: When I took the first pictures there was a couple spots where we couldn't really spend time, like Indian Point. That's why I came back up on the following weekend.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Mm-hmm (affirmative).

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: To get photographs and did a little fishing and stuff.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: See, we weren't always successful in the early days. We didn't get fir in and we had all those patches.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: They missed their chance.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Did you do that last one?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah, back there on that last ten acres you can see a whole bunch of alder.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Oh.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Before modern herbicides starting being, some of the older herbicides weren’t really effective.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Mm-hmm (affirmative).

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: It was products like Krenite that didn't do much for the salmonberries.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: You got salmonberry here but you've also got scotch broom and Himalayan blackberries.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah. The scotch broom and Himalayan has not really been here until the last 20 years. It’s all just arriving.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Ah-hah. So it's real recent.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Real recent. They were down in the bottom from the homesteads. But it's moved up slope with the roads and birds and everything.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: On this part of the forest, almost all of the crushed rock came from local quarries, so we mustn’t forget that. Hauled in from Reedsport. Umpqua rock. And that’s where the scotch broom is coming from.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: If you drive by those [rock] piles at Reedsport you'll still see stacks of them.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yep.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: This is what it looks like after I sprayed through here last year.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Uh-huh.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: You mean the road sides too?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yep.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: It would be a lot more solid if I hadn't been controlling it.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: What are the specifications now on reforestation?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Well . . .

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Do you do it on a grid or micro-sites, or what kind of spacing do you use today?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Spacing varies. For a while we were planting a nine-foot spacing in which there's 538 trees per acre.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: For many years, they did ten-by at 436. A couple years back we came up a little short of trees so went down to 11-by at 360.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: You can be successful at all of those, your likelihood of being successful with red cedar and hemlock in the mix is probably better at 9-by.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: If you're using mostly fir, about 10 or 11 is what works. It depends on where you're going with the stand. If you're going to harvest it at 40 years and more trees are needed out there than we do for 130 years.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: What density per acre at a 130?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I really can't tell you.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Was it higher?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: 80 or 100, easy.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: We left beyond the Carlson Hillside. Yeah, take a right. Nobody grows trees at 130 years anymore.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: If you're going at 40, what's the stem count at 40 that you're looking for?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Industry seems to want 450 per acre.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow. 450 at 40 years of age?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: The target age is 65.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: In Lincoln County Georgia-Pacific clearcut one of my plantations at 22 years.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Really? Fir?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: On the 1000 Line out of Toledo.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Huh.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I was shocked. It was a conversion from grassland to plantation with Doug fir plug-1 seedlings.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Mm-hmm (affirmative).

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: We never had any problem with Swiss needle cast.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Well, I know we have had incidences . . .

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Mmm?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: . . . with Swiss needle cast.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh, okay.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: We never had it disappear down here, but up there --

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: We had a lot of trouble planting hemlock stock. It takes special stock to transplant it.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Mm-hmm (affirmative).

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: How do you work around that?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: It seems to, if you take care of it, you need to plant it faster than you did Doug fir. You need to have it at an the early part of the cycle to get it in the ground sooner.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Other than that, if you get it planted right, it grows fairly well.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: When the weather's right.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: The wind's been blowing, it's been raining, something's coming down.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yeah. [illegible speaking/tape beeping 42:03 to 42:23]

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: . . . Douglas fir is cheaper than the other, and if you get it in at the right time, it provides them a lot of chewing but not for the deer or elk.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Huh!

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Doug fir only gets chewed on the first year or so for the most part because it’s harder on them. Whereas, red cedar they'll chew on for six to seven years. I was looking awhile back thinking where we were doing successful with red cedar, and I noticed we were being successful with red cedar where we were used Big Game Repellant [BGR] on them.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh. We just started using it toward the end of my career, and we were calling it “BGR.”

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: We didn't know if that worked or not.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: What's that made from?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Well there are a number of things. They make it out of chicken eggs, they make it out of animal blood.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Guts.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: You know.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Something smelly.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah, and it has to taste bad. There's probably hot sauce in a Mexican restaurant, that seems to do just fine with some folks, that might work around here. No one else likes it. It’s like throwing money away. I always liked to think the Elk spoke with a Spanish accent. (Laughs)

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: (Laughs)

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: They like the flavor.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Si, si, senor!

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah, we were just trying it, we didn't know if it was going to be successful or not but we did the staking-and-tubing, and bud-capping and different strategies.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: The blood product seems to work best.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: They really don't want to be around it.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: They're vegetarians, so . . .

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Right.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Anything that smells like dead meat kind of repels them I think.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I always wondered if it was attracting bears to eat it! (Laughs)

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: There you go. They seem to be only a problem on larger trees. Do you have any problems with bears here?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: We haven't had problems with bear here. It’s been north of Umpqua and south of Coquille that they’ve been having problems.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: And it seems to be moving this way but so far we haven't had problems.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Huh!

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: We've tried to keep the bear population from the houses and attacking residents.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh. How about the cougar and bobcat populations, are those coming back?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I don't know that there's any shortage of either one of those.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh. So, they are back.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I've seen two or three bobcats on different days at times, but you see them every few months and you'll see one and then you'll see two in one day.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Bears are the same way. You see them every so often.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Has that increase in cat populations, has that had any effect on the boomer population does it seem?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I don't think it does. It helps but I don't think it's something that we count on.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Maybe that's why we don't have as many animals on the east side of the forest because they've all settled west.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: What was the reason?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: He's asking about bobcats, cougar, and coyotes, and stuff that prey on mountain beaver.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: And I'm thinking, where are we on that? The only place we don't have a lot of those is right on the edge.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Why do you think that is?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I have no idea.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh. Jerry, when they had the blow-down from the Columbus Day storm --

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Mm-hmm (affirmative).

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Then they had, the real serious damage on Elliott was on the west side.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Primarily.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Close to the ocean.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Primarily.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: But then Weyerhaeuser had a lot of damage too, and they're inland.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yep. They didn't have . . . it was mostly on the west side.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh, okay, same thing then?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Uh-huh.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: These western slopes have a lot of shallow soil areas and stand rot in some places where they didn't have any roots to hold on in that kind of a wind. It's the only day I've ever seen dirt blow sideways with the wind.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: (Laughs)

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So you can remember Columbus Day.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I can remember Columbus Day Storm.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I can too. I was at a high school in Portland with powerlines and falling trees.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I think that's our third hurricane. Up to that day, we'd been tying baggies to rocks with string and throwing it in the air. It was a parachute back then. We lost all of our baggies that day. (Laughs)

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Ah-hah. (Laughs)

entries.text: Lionel’s [Youst] has given us permission to put all three of those books online, on the website.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I'm glad for that. The communication between the on-the-ground surveyors and the GLO office are very interesting because they're being personal decisions. It's just between people like this have to be taught.

entries.text: Holy cow! This [road] is curvy.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Welcome to my world. Mark [Huff, Titan-Kelly LLC] asked me to drive this road to home every night. I said no. (Laughter)

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: All our roads in eastern Oregon are straight, so this is a good balance.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Three times a month is more than enough.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I really miss traveling in the woods every day. I thought when I went to school that I'd be spending a lot more time in the woods. Just the opposite.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Well, you know, you have those moments where something happens and you look around and realize the beauty you're in. Some of them are ridge top moments and some of them canyon bottom moments when you go out and cross that waterfall.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: We used to have what we had called a “contemplating life” moment, when you almost get hit by a tree or barely your get your truck around a landslide.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Or they drive you in a van.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Who does most of the planting now? Is it local contractors or is it . . .?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: This year is going to be a local contract. Last year was Medford, the year before was a guy -- five years before that, four or five years in a row, it was a guy out of Salem.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: What was his name?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Fremont Forest Systems, was a five-year contractor. Escalante Reforestation was the guy last year, and this year it looks like ride tree services.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I'm guessing Medford and Salem are Mexican crews?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: And some of the guys on ride tree services are too, but I don't know.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: And everybody knows that a good portion of those people are all illegal?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Do they?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well, they tried to cover it up but I think it's common knowledge, isn't it?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Well, you know, some of them were brought in by a new process. They have a visa -- work visa -- that they seem to be able to get the state

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: department to approve people coming across the border to work. I don't know if that's going to continue with the new administration or not. And yes, there were some illegals on crews over the years. There were some criminals on crews over the years.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yep, I used to belong to Associate Reforestation Contractors, and so we did a little bit of an investigation on some of the labor we employed [in the 1970s]. 100% of the Mexican crews were illegal and some of the owners were illegal, and they were being counted as “diversity employees” by the Forest Service in central Oregon: “oh, we got a diverse employment force.” We got -- except they called them colored people [“people of color”] or something.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I was never told that I should check that out. We should take a left if we’re going down Sullivan.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: It was a real problem and it ended up pretty much destroying the reforestation industry as we knew it by having illegals come in and low bid and . . .

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah. Well . . .

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Got rid of all the locals.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I started just as that was happening and there weren't a lot of white guys that were willing to work that hard.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well, we didn't have any trouble. I had guys work twelve, fifteen years [inaudible, odd noise 00:05:40]. [inaudible: tape noise 5:39 to 6:22]

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Exactly. It's just like farm crops.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: They're paying a lot right now to keep the crews together.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yep. Well, if they become legal there'll be a lot more payroll. There’s a whole lot of politics behind it, and the primary people that brought them in and maintained employment was the federal government. Private landowners weren't using them for a lot of years.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Really?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well, it was a problem with insurance. Compensation insurance that a private land owner is liable. State and feds could care less.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Weyerhaeuser doesn't seem to worry about it.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: No, they had to finally give up. I planted five years in the '60s. I remember one Mexican tree planter and I hired several on my crew. They all had documentation. Weyerhaeuser turned me on to them and after two or three years, I found out their documentation was forged, and by that time they're friends and family and long-time employees.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: That's one of the things I heard. They had green cards and visas for some of these guys, but a lot's basically changed.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well, they had a whole industry. At Tacoma they had a lawyer that routinely issued phony IDs for those guys.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: You can stop right about here. Somewhere around here, 10 feet away maybe.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: And look to the left. That's why we were amazed that reforestation was so difficult. It looked to us like okay, this is all natural. It was a hundred square miles of just natural, fully stocked, fir regrowth. All we got to do is harvest, light a match, go home, and in comes a fully-stocked stand of young fir. And it turned out it wasn't that way.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Were you leaving seed trees?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: No. We're leaving just a clearcut, hundred acres here, hundred acres there, and really, it's not that simple. Up came salmonberry and thimbleberry and alder, and boomers. Then, oh, yeah! you got to go up there and do some planting -- and that was a real revelation. It seemed so simple. It wasn't just on our ground, it was the Siuslaw National Forest. The whole Siuslaw, clear to Corvallis, was one solid block of natural-grown fir.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Obviously, all you had to do was harvest the material and then watch it re- grow, you know? No, it's not that simple. We never did understand why. Never did understand why.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: We still don't, do we?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: We know the fire was a huge part of that, but even when you burn a north slope or a west slope, it didn’t do anything regarding natural reforestation -- and yet here it was. A natural thing. So that I guess we never did fully understand.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: And probably never will.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Probably never will.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: The size of the fire made a difference in that it killed a lot of stuff on its way through, so high, and you know the mountain beaver probably didn't survive as well as they do when we do a slash burn.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach

Balloon logging downhill had the obvious disadvantage of heavy winds. You had to shut down if there's heavy winds, storms, mechanical problems -- I heard that even vandalism went on.
