entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: They are really bad tasting.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: You just didn't prepare it right.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: They don't taste like chicken?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: No, they are real fishy and grainy and not good.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Taste buds are like the eye of the beholder, different taste buds.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well, it's like caviar or something, yeah, it's an acquired taste. Some of the tribes, some of the Indians, preferred eel over salmon. Because salmon was so common and ordinary over a long time.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Eel is how hungry they are.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: They didn't get as much.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Eels were greasy and stuff, too. High fat content was important.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I guess the Indians up around in the Columbia, they preferred to eat dog instead of salmon.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: They like salmon, but dog's a little better.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I remember Lewis and Clark got in a fight with one Indian because he was mocking them for eating dogs. They were raising dogs for wool and Lewis and Clark preferred dog over elk.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yep, they did.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: But some of the Indian tribes thought it was real primitive to be eating dog, they didn't think that was right. Like eating children, or something.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well, I’ve talked to several people about the eel runs and you’re the first one that has verified them, that's been recent. They’re still there.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: The guy who didn't cook eel badly, you cross over Lamprey Creek, named for lamprey eels. That's the old name.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Coquille is from Skwakol, which is the Chinook name for eel. They had a, in 1851 or 52 somebody went in, one of the first white parties to go into upper Coquille River and the Indians were gathered where Myrtle Point is, hundreds of them, harvesting eels.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: So it was like the county fair to them.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah, yeah. So there's a park down there, too, I can't think of the name of it right now [Laverne County Park]. It's got a myrtlewood grove in it, old- growth, falls, and that was another spot where they would gather for eels.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I'm not sure if that's an endangered species yet, but it just might be one.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I think them and mountain beaver deserve to be endangered more than spotted owls. If you want to go on actual danger and limited range.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Some of us are trying to plant trees and prefer you not go there. I don't know if we can come up with a [protective] tube to keep the mountain beavers out.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah, we stake-and-tubed lots of trees and they would get all the branches on the side, climb up to the top, and pick the top off.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah, I've seen them cut a hole in the tube and take the tree out.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Enough for Robert's Ridge, or go up to Scholfield?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Did we go out Robert's Ridge before? It seemed like we were on at least a portion of it.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yeah, just not very far.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's where I was trying to show you the myrtle grove.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh, right. But we only went out just a short distance.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It's probably gone.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah, but it was a bench below us there.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Right.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: The only thing we've lost on the recording is Balti's home site and then some of the discussion of spawning gravel as we were moving. And when we hit the Old Maid's Cabin, we were good again. So from Gould's Lake to Old Maid's Cabin, that was the tape I screwed up.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Ah, yes.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: But fortunately it wasn't a major stop or anything else. We did Robert's Ridge and the Divide Camp and all that, and Dean's Mountain and -- was it called Mud Lake Waterhole, or Muddy Waterhole?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Muddy Flats, it seems like.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Muddy Flats, okay, ‘cause we did get two or three different names on that. I wanted to . . .

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It was the Dean’s Mountain water source.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: We can stop there if you want to redo the photos that you had rained on at Dean Mountain.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Dean Mountain? Is that very far out of the way?

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Nope, that's right on the way.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: That would be wonderful, now I really wish I had my other camera. Except I'll know where the location is and this actually does take pretty decent pictures. I had a 35 mm. camera for about 30 years, I took thousands of photos with it, and somebody stole it. So I went over to digital and I've never gone back. Digital in the first few years wasn't very good. But now, these old cameras are better than the 35 mm.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Your cellphones now take phenomenal pictures.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah, mine's a five [iPhone], it's an older one. I hardly could use it for two or three years. I've done one or two videos on it and it's taken a few hundred photos and it takes very nice photos.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: It does.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Jerry, that picture I took of you and David and Wayne at the [Jerry Phillips] reserve there? That came out real well.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Oh, I'm glad.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: And that was with a phone. That's why, have you gone to the website, the Elliott website they put up?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: No, my computer crashed a while back. It’s not fully functioning yet.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-oh. But you're getting emails?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I am.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: But you can't use the links to go on to the website?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Not yet.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh, okay. I was going too send you some more links, but I'll wait for you to get there.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Now how old is this reprod here; 25-, 30-years old?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So it would be 29, yep. And where are we right now?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Dry Lake used to be right here. You could take a trail over here. You got Benson Creek down that draw.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: And we went along Benson Creek, didn't we? Or just the ridgeline?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Just the ridgeline.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: These ones have had a lot of scotch broom grown in over the years, too.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Looks like there's an old loggers camp or hunters camp there, too.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Mm-hmm (affirmative).

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: This is Dry Ridge, and there's . . . yeah, the CC’s spike camp on some of these flats.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: One thing I keep forgetting about, the tree progeny test sites on the forest. Will we go by any of them today?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: There's one on Sullivan Ridge and one on Larson, off the 2000.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That’s on Totten Creek. And the third one is over there on Cougar Ridge.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah. So, no, they're all behind us.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay. I don't have my notes. They'll have to go in my memory.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Me too. I've spent enough time in progeny test sites, I remember where they're all at.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Ah, while, I'd like to get them on a map or location and track them by aerial photos or something of that nature. On the Yaquina, me and a neighbor set up our own progeny test sites on our own land, but I wasn't able to afford to keep them long enough.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Well, we did one thinning.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Stay left?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Stay left, if you want to go down to the 8000.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: If we’re going to Dean Mountain, we don’t have that far.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Have we been by this point before?

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay, and I think we got a good discussion of this alder; this is the one that hasn't changed for forty or fifty years and I got a nice photo of it. And was that, was the intersection back there was that --?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Joe’s Ridge.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay, but was that where the Divide Camp was?

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: And so there's a spring just off to the right there, a little bit.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yeah, there was a softball field.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Is that where that was at?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yep, this is Dry Lake.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: But that's back there a little ways?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Just a little ways.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Maybe there was a cabin that's fit that description. The 8000 road and --

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: There were some CC cabins there.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Do we want to eat lunch? It's noon?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: We're pretty close to the lookout, aren't we? Or are we going there or not?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: We're going towards there.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Just a few miles.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Should we have lunch there, maybe?

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Works for me.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: The lookout is a smidge past the Scholfield turn, but we can stop up there and hang out and then backtrack back and go out Dean Creek.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: It's pretty recent, this reprod through here. Probably five or seven years old?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Probably five. Five and six.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So this is one of the most recent logging jobs?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: No, we have some stuff that we haven't planted yet and 400 acres from last year.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Are these supposed to be riparian trees there or something?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yes. Very expensive.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah, a lot of money sitting there.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yes there is. What's it doing?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: It's supposed to be shading the stream, so the water temperature in the main stream doesn't go up in the summertime.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: [Mike] Newton did a lot of research on that and they showed that if you take that right down to the stream bank, the stream temperature doesn't go up. That's the theory, but that's --

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Others disagree with him on that.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well, they do, but they don't have anything backing them up, there's no measurements anywhere.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I can't argue with that (laughter). That's not the most expensive buffer we’ve got.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: They don't differentiate between which side of the creek it's on, either.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Nope. North side of the creek doesn't give it any shade and they don't take into account the lack of transpiration. And that's a big deal. Even where the blackberries grow up they'll dry up a stream in the summer.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: You are right.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: There’s that pallet.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: That's what happens when you do forestry from a computer.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: So you move that pallet around you'll get really confused.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: You will. Yeah. What really messes me up is when they move it somewhere else.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: A lot of this is all planted on this side.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So the 400 acres this year, you'll plant to hemlock and Doug fir, at ten-foot spacing?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: The initials this year are only 72 acres and yeah, we'll be on percentage. Mostly Doug fir but some western hemlock, some cedar. There's the company land, five units where they're planning it; we'll put more trees back in for sure.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: What's your survival rate on hemlock?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: You know, I've never tracked it -- straight ahead. I've never tracked it and it varies so much from year to year, depending on how you treat it. I planted some last year that I thought wasn't going to do very well and it did fine as far as I can tell. It was a unit up on Monday and down to the buffer, so we put in hemlock around the buffer.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Interesting.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: They don't have an issue with shade, but they're not a lot better than Douglas fir for trying to grow in salmonberry and stuff like that.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Salmonberry kills almost everything you put under it. The only possible exception might be red cedar.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Spruce might.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Spruce might, if you get enough sunlight, yeah.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: But wouldn't you spray the salmonberry, prior to planting?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Where you can, yes. But if it's in a stream buffer, then you can't do that.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Got it.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: With the helicopter, the buffer is wider.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: We did spot treatment by hand. In a lot of places it's cheaper than a helicopter.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Really?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: That's what we would do, mulch it, spray it, and burn it. Maybe do a follow up spray or, hardly ever need a replant once we got our systems down.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: It was pretty good until the state nursery closed and they started bringing in contractors to grow trees for us.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: We established the quality of those trees compared to Georgia-Pacific or Weyerhaeuser’s.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Seemed like they saved their special stuff for us, being the state.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: That's probably true. And there's a lot of giveaways at the end of the year and people are planting off-site seedlings.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah, we had this one manager who'd take over his own business from time to time instead of this manager whose employees wouldn't, so he decided to do it himself. He didn't understand that you have to do things when you have to do it. So he didn't do some of the steps or doing it at the wrong time, and lost a lot of trees. 1500 out of 100,000 will last longer, that were big enough.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow. That was our problem with the 2-0s from the [D.L.] Phipps Nursery. They were real small, and we just found out that it was way more costly to try to baby undersized seedlings or poor seedlings to create a free-to-grow state than it was just to start with a good seedling in the first place.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: There was a point from about 1985 on that they got pretty good at what they did. They had occasional problems, but you get an awful lot of stock out of there if you get a nice one and set it in the ground. The specs were good.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah, that was the other thing. If we didn't have good site-prep to grow good quality seedlings. So we had it down to a pretty good science until everything went gunny bag; until the spotted owl flew in; until they created buffers.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Well, one of the early things they found out; if a tree was as big as your thumb it might have a limb left on it that a mountain beaver would go up to the top and get some more. Anything smaller than that, you'll chew off at the very first limb.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: We had to stake-and-tube, or stake-and-carton were boomer was. Did you ever use staking-and-tubing or staking-and-cartoning?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Staking-and-tubing we did when I first got here. Then they went to free- standing tubes and we didn't put a stake in there.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Did you have trouble with maintaining the tube?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: There was some issues, but we didn't usually maintain it. The issues were the elk would drag them down the hill, as long as they'd leave us the tree.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: The thing that surprised me, I'd be at progeny test sites and I staked and tubed them and I came back 20 years later and some of the trees were almost totally girdled by the tubes. The tubes didn't break down like they said they were supposed to.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: The first round of tubes didn't break down and they looked at the yellow plastic in the sunlight. I've seen some of those on a previous plantation -- that big there is just too restricted for plastic.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yep, I've seen a few like that. But they never did, those were supposed to break down in two or three years, but they didn't.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Depends on the amount of sunlight they get. You get a good tree, it'll shade the sun away and it lasts a long time.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: That's precisely what happened.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: After this next run at your left, it's blocked, has a gorse patch down there that I haven't gotten to in the last year or two. Somebody made it so I couldn't get a 4-track down it, we had other priority work, I didn't walk down there.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: What ridgeline is this right here?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Oh, that's a spur ridge, I don't know the name of that one.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It's with Scholfield.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Got a bit of an east wind up here.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yep.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Weather's looking good through next Tuesday.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's what brings the clear weather in.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Won’t rain at all!

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's Oregon weather.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: What creates the temperature inversion in the Willamette Valley is the fog.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Do you want to get out here? Do you want to eat here?

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yeah, let’s go a little further.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yeah, that way.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: That'll take you to Dean Mountain.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Or we could eat and then we'll drive that way, we'll do a little backtracking, but.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well, last time we came up here the visibility was about 30 feet.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: You'll see further today.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: The stand down the hill and we pruned that, there's something. Get some clear wood out of it and keeps you from thinking of going out on a loss.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So you've done pruning up here on the stand?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Quite a few.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Has that improved the value of the trees?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Our economist in 1987 told us we were getting some exercise but that's all we could get out of it. So we quit doing that.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well, economists are pretty notorious for making poor predictions. I wonder if they turned out to be true.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I have no idea. I think one of the things you have to wait long enough -- this might be a good spot right here -- you have to wait long enough to find out what you made money with. I think you're going to cut with the value.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Why don't we go up to the tower? Then I can get the shots that replicate the Osborne's.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Do you have keys?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: They got keys.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: We should grab a key.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: So this is what I have trouble dealing with.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: It should be the same lock.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Really?

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yep.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Didn't used to be.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: We've got a nest under here, too.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: One of the early trappings for the International Scout came up over the weekend. Probably for the same reason.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Oh, okay.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: It’s kind of windy at the top.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Last time we were up here you couldn't see any of this.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Beautiful view.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: If you know which one, you can see Roman Nose from here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I take the pictures then I go back later and look at the map and see what I'm looking at. I’ve taken about 25 or 30 of the Osbornes on the lookouts and then gone in and labeled them, the different landmarks above them, and then put them online, so that everyone can see them and see what it looked like, back then.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: It's pretty irritating in a way. You go and you get good old maps, like Jerry’s got there, and Osborne photos and the General Land Office surveys, and they don't match the spotted owl projections. Here's how it used to be, here's what we’re trying to create, and here's how we're going to do it. And if you've been around very long ago, that's all nonsense, and then after a while it's not.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: The thing is, they took what they thought the spotted owl needed and then multiplied it by ten times to figure how much they needed for him and make sure that nothing went wrong with the claim.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: We've all been here since day one, and they didn't need second-growth forest -- and now what they're trying to protect is second-growth forest. They changed the rules somehow.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: The ologists said that, these owls now they're here, but they're unhappy. They want to go back to the Weyerhaeuser old-growth, but they're sitting here unhappily.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: With stories from --

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: You don't want unhappy owls.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: They know that because they've got a frown on their beak?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I think that's it.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I think they know that because they have an agenda on the plate. They've been very successful.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: They have.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So this is the first time you've been up here in a while, Roger?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Um, I walked this last year around the back side posting the spray paint check. And I was down on that point, looking to stand over probably in May.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Last time I was here was the first time I'd ever been here and the first time -- Jerry, you said you hadn't been here in 20 or 30 years.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: This is one of the first places I was on the forest had to get a load of tubes out of here one time. [crosstalk]

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: It's always interesting being up here a moment before daylight and seeing the fishing boats out there with those huge lights shining.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Ah-hah.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: This is a view, huh?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: It's blowing 30.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: You can really see the forest and the trees out there, can’ you?

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Mm-hmm (affirmative).
Stop #C-17. 28:20 Scholfield Waterhole & Road Numbers. No Photos.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: On your left, when we planted it last year -- so it has probably kept doing okay..

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: How about on the right here? Jerry, do you know something . . .?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Hmmm?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: That was done before I got here, probably . . . probably sometime in the mid-70s would be my guess.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: It looks like a 50 or 60-year old plantation.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Do you have to take time off work to do this, Roger, or is this just part of your job?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I don't know (laughter). We didn't discuss it. But I know I've been working more hours than they intended this year.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Are you the sole employee for reforestation?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Mm-hmm (affirmative). The original plan was that I'd work about 320 hours and I probably had it in last month, easy. It was way beyond that point.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: 320 hours total?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Normally.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: What are your thoughts on the state not managing it anymore?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I don't have a political answer to that.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: The tape is going, but you will have a chance to . . . I usually warn you before I ask for an opinion. (laughter)

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Amber, what's my opinion on ODF not managing it anymore?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Ask Randy, he is the master.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Of no opinion?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Of no opinion: “I don't have enough information at this time.”

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Well, Roger, there's nothing you can do about it, it's up to the landlord.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I was not interested in retiring at that point, but you know. It just came about that way.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So on a personal level, you'd want to keep working the way it was?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I could do with two or three more years. It would have made it more comfortable when I retired, financially.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: You and Jerry and Marv Rawley are very few of the people I've talked to anymore that did their whole career basically on one forest.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yep. Well, I had work I did in forests before here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: But 35 years, a good portion of your career.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: You feel fortunate that you've been able to spend all that time here, or . . .?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Oh, I loved most of it. Yes.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Ah-hah. It seems to be the opinion of people who have worked a piece of land until they knew it real well.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I did some logging for seven or eight summers before I started. Then I was with the Forest Service for two summers . . . and so far nobody I've ever worked for said they wouldn't hire me back!

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Ah-hah. Department of Forestry.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Well, I think I'm getting too old for them. I think if I had been 30 they would have offered me a position in the agency. When you get over 60, people look at you, “You want to work yet? Why?” (laughter).

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I went back to college so I wouldn't have to retire.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I made more as a tree planter than I did as a researcher. By a ways.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: There's not many reforesters in their forties. Working full time in reforestation, in this country.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Nope. Yep, that’s true.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: ‘Cause your knees and your back will eventually give out.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Why I'm doing better in a truck.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: There you go. Well, then you can use mechanized equipment, on a flat like they do in the south.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: One of the employees was down there and asked one of their guys, '”How come your sales boundaries are so far off the ground, ten feet in the air?” “Well, that's how deep the snow was when we posted it.”

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: We did a pre-commercial thinning unit on hemlock, outside of Tacomah [Washington] on Weyerhaeuser, and all the trees were real bushy up to about ten, twelve foot and then they're just dead. Just level. That's the level of snow and then they had rabbits up there eating the tops off year after year. It was one of the weird looking area.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Snowshoe hare?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I don't know, that's what they told us, rabbit damage from the winter.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: This is the waterhole up here, too.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Now which waterhole is this one?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I think we called it Scholfield Creek Waterhole.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yep, it is.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Did we stop here before?

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Can we get a reading here, Amber?

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yeah, we can take a quick look at it.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: All of these ridgelines and the waterholes are lining up north and south for hundreds of thousands of acres. You can just tell right where people camped out and the travel routes to get in between these areas. It's kind of surprising; they're rarely ever more than three or five miles apart. About an hour apart, worst case.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Are you doing a history of pre-European civilization?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: What's that?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Are you doing a history of pre-?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: That's pretty much what I focus on, is . . . well, if Amber can take the picture, I don't have to move.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: We noticed anything here, we assumed there may be water here. No bass. (laughter)

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Thank God.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: One of the biologists from Fish and Wildlife asked me, “Do you have any fish in these waterholes?” And she was looking for herbicide sources and I said, “Not unless they can walk or fly.” (laughter)

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: A lot of the Cascade lakes were fish-free, and then they hiked them in, on purpose.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah. Fishermen.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: They can't live on the river, so they do it every year. Hiking into the high lakes.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah, well, the Cascades, some of those lakes have fish in them. Now what's this waterhole called again?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I think it's Scholfield.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Its Scholfield.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: And Scholfield has an L in there?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That is the historic question, Amber, going back 60 years: should it or shouldn't it?

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: It just washed up an r.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It's a portable size.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Do you want to waste an l or not?

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: ‘Cause you only get so many l's in your life, and you don't want to use them all up.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: They use the l on the north side of town, and take it out on the south side.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: There's a book called [Lewis] Macarthur's book of [Oregon] Geographic Names that's helpful, ‘cause he gives you the reason.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It's interesting how often in Oregon, little towns were named for the first name of some guy's wife.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah. Marys Peak.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Josephine County.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: That's a daughter, though.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: There’s a bunch of them.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah. That's funny, you cross the Columbia and you go up to Washington, and it's mostly Indian names.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: There are up here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: And you come down here and, except for the rivers, very few Indian names.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Some, but not as many.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Not nearly as many. And a lot more white settler names in western Oregon.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Some of them in Oregon were post mistresses.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: You look at the left hand side, this was a big alder patch.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh, so this has been converted?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Been converted into fir.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: That looks pretty successful.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Big Creek had a lot of that here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: My crews did a lot of alder conversion over a ten- or twelve-year period in Lincoln County and a little bit in Washington. That's the main thing we did.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Did we make money on the timber sale, if it was an alder conversion?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Barely. About ‘61 alder became, it had a positive value on the appraisal sheet, but not much. Maybe a dollar.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: I remember going out with the timber inventory team and they were counting them a dollar a tree. That was in ‘86.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: In the 30s, alder was worth more than Douglas fir.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Really?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well, if it was same diameter. They would use them for furniture at B. P. John’s in Portland, and stuff like that. Or firewood or whatever. Doug fir just didn't have any value to it.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Alder, the last time I looked, it was anything over twelve inches 900 dollars a thousand.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Alder?

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Alder.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: So it's value went up pretty drastically the last couple of years. But you only grow half as many thousand board feet to the acre.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Of course, you can get there quicker. And it's got an entirely different product.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: My great uncle was a timber cruiser and he bought a section of hemlock up by – I can’t think of the town’s name [Centralia], it’s up past Brush Prairie {Washington], near the Olympia area.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Hmm! (startled)

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Something fell off.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Can you get it back? [crosstalk, recorder turned off/on]

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: . . . just kind of fell in the line, that 1100, 1200, it's all just, it was just called “rational.” But as far as the 2000 -- it's an important road, too, that's the old Dry Ridge Road -- but the others, 5-, 6-, 700; those are all just arbitrary. No reason for them.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: What was the reason they decided to do that, then?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I don't recall ever hearing that discussion. It was after I retired.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh, so they hadn't numbered the roads?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So they've been numbered since 1990.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's it, since 1990.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow. So what road are we going down, is this still the old --

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Scholfield Ridge.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay. Well, your career straddled going from the names to the numbers.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Then, too, the high school kids starting stealing the signs that had names on them. Taking it home, putting it in their garage or bedroom, wherever it was.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Just kind of a trophy.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: He wasn't interested in stealing the 1200 or 1530 or something like that. I kind of liked the names.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well, I know in the Valsetz area Boise-Cascade kept putting up signs. The roads are just like this here, if you don't know them, they all look the same. But the locals were stealing them because they didn't want people coming in there. It wasn't high school kids, it was loggers.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: People fishing back at the lake.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: The [Siletz] gorge there, you can get into the lake from Dallas, but from the gorge side . . . or have you ever been to the Valley of the Giants?

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Oh, yeah.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I have not.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I went up there the first weekend they designated that, just to see what they were doing. I haven't been back there in probably 20 years though; quite a few times.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: How big a piece of land is that?

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Not very big, it's like 40 or 80 acres. Like Jerry's Private Reserve. Just about the same. More of a bench, more sloping, bigger trees. But they’re probably up to 500 years old, I think. The biggest one in there fell over, after they designated it.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: It was the same thing; Boise-Cascade drained the lake.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: They used to have a joke for a while: they should stop designating the biggest one because then it will fall over. It's happened three or four times.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Finnegan's Fir; the spruce out of Seaside.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yep. But here’s kind of a typical pole stand. They had peelings of pole pilings, but then you couldn't get in some parts around the curves; we had tight corners and curves.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: And then you cut the corner you could make? Back then we had a guy sitting in the back of the rig, driving the back axle. Haven't seen one of those in a few years.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: There’s a lot more diversity out here than I expected.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Jerry, do you know why this is called Twin Sisters, up here?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: You know, I never heard. Although people who lived at the mouth of Smith River over there, I got acquainted with some of them. And you can see that, from where they live. It was kind of a ridgeline aberration, and it may have been named by people up there.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: It had two little peaks on it?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yeah, they were not prominent. But from a distance, they were recognized.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: We probably flattened it out a little bit when we cut the trees out.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: But we had never named anything for them, because they're not prominent.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: How about that clearcut down over there? That looks pretty recent.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: That's one we planted last year. In Scholfield: Part 51 and Part 52. We found out last week that I reversed the sides. I don't know if anybody else got that. Hopefully they hadn't done any work on it.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: There's a nice patch through here. This the 130-year-old stuff again? That is remarkable, how it all came in solid fir like that; pretty solid.

entries.speaker: Roger Johnson
entries.text: Mm-hmm. (affirmative)

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Because the ground had to have been cleared enough that the seeds could provide a seed bed. If you had a fire, that killed all the trees, but it didn't clear the ground, you wouldn’t have a seed bed.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah. It looks like there's repeat fires. So the 1840 fire, we don't know what the extent was.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: We do not know that.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So the 1868 could have been a reburn, in a way.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I think part of it was.

entries.text: And so part of that whole transaction was that we got to choose about 400 acres of land that the sanctuary had out there to make the transaction stay whole in the eyes of the Land Board. entries.text: made our choice. I spent, I don't know how many thousand dollars I spent. Probably $30,000 at least. I sent my engineers out there to locate all the property lines for that 400 acres that we believed that we got. What are we talking about?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: They were in total denial. So Norma [Kline]got stuck with the job of dealing with a frustrated Land Board how to solve that. But it's only going to solve through money, not through land. So the Land Board never was made whole for the transfer of its land base.
